extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing creative writers (especially those interested in horror and queer-centered work), writing students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and craft principles for writing horror and formally inventive fiction, with emphasis on using form (lists, structure), personal fears, and queer perspectives as generative material. Includes classroom exercises and practical guidance on sentence-level rigor and source engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of list-making as a formal device
rubrics_metrics.description: “List making itself is sort of a queer form, or a form that’s queered... To me a list is a fluid and liminal form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists can be practical (grocery) or poetical; they are a legitimate structural choice to shape an essay or story. Consider using a series of theses or numbered items to zero in on a subject (e.g., Machado’s 'Nine Theses' on refrigerator horror). Lists can foreground fragmentation, liminality, and multiplicity; they are a deliberate formal move, not a shortcut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin from form or concept and zero in
rubrics_metrics.description: “I think about an idea or a concept or a form, and then begin to zero in on the thing as I’m moving towards it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a formal constraint or conceptual lens as the entry point for a piece (e.g., the fridge as portal/coffin). Let the form guide what you notice and what you develop rather than starting only from plot. This is a repeatable compositional strategy for assignments and commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunt motifs and concrete recurring images through research
rubrics_metrics.description: Machado describes 'hunting down every single [example of] refrigerators in other movies' to define the sub-genre of 'fridge horror.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively gather examples across media to identify shared qualities (portals, temporal effects) and use that corpus to articulate what connects works. This is both analytical research and inspiration for making compositional choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use horror to interrogate fear as a measure of self/society
rubrics_metrics.description: “To learn what we fear is to learn who we are... Fear is the oldest emotion... it connects us to the most ancient part of what makes a human human.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat horror as a diagnostic genre: map personal and historical anxieties to illuminate character and cultural moments. Effective horror links private terrors to broader social or historical conditions rather than relying solely on shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center queer experience in horror rather than making queerness the target of fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Machado emphasizes placing queer identities at the focal center of horrifying narratives, noting horror’s historical tendency to manifest as 'fear of the queer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write queer characters and desires as subjects (complex, interior), not just as monstrous otherness. Exploit horror’s affinity for the ineffable to represent desires and experiences that historically lacked language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory personal fears as a generative exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: As a classroom assignment Machado makes students write a hundred fears to access deeper, less obvious anxieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push past surface fears (spiders) to find idiosyncratic, intense items that reveal individual voice and material. Allow redaction or a private version for sensitive items; the list is a tool for the writer’s discovery, not mandatory public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground horror in self-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: “I can tell when I’ve read horror by somebody who’s never really looked at themselves very closely... The horror I respond to is where this person has taken stock of themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic horror often comes from authors who have interrogated their own fears, experiences, and limits. Avoid generic scares that lack personal specificity; strive for material that bears the author's psychological imprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push boundaries and embrace productive discomfort
rubrics_metrics.description: “Learning how to push your own boundaries, learning how to be uncomfortable; like being uncomfortable can be so productive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discomfort as a creative resource: take artistic risks to unsettle both writer and reader. Recognize the ethical and emotional responsibility (especially in classroom settings) when prompting or publishing uncomfortable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use influence-dialogue with source texts thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing in relation to Shirley Jackson, Machado 'wrote a story... in conversation with' Jackson’s work, explicitly engaging with scenes and characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what you’re taking from a predecessor (tone, motif, scene) and translate it through your perspective—this can be homage, fan-fiction, or formal conversation. Be conscious of what technical devices you’re adapting and how your piece converses rather than simply imitates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and structure as the primary route into stories
rubrics_metrics.description: “Form and structure is so important, I can’t escape it... it is just the way I get into most things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately choose or invent structural systems (e.g., lists, constrained forms, fragmented chronology) as a means to generate narrative and thematic meaning. Treat form as generative rather than decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read analytically—'harvest' formal elements from other work
rubrics_metrics.description: “When I read anything I feel like I’m just harvesting... what’s making this thing work, structurally speaking...?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate reading practices that focus on structure, sentences, and formal moves. Annotate how effects are achieved so you can repurpose those techniques in your own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous sentence-level craft: 'sit harder on your sentences'
rubrics_metrics.description: Machado recounts a teacher: 'you need to sit harder on your sentences... they need to be really good because they are literally the thing I’m building the building out of.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize sentence revision and precision; view sentences as the building blocks of fiction. Avoid letting 'slack' sentences accumulate—polish syntax, diction, rhythm, and clarity as central to literary effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge identity without reducing the work to it ('both/and')
rubrics_metrics.description: Machado articulates a duality: identity (queer, woman, Latina) is inseparable from the artist but not the only thing that defines the work: 'forget I am a lesbian. And second, never forget I am a lesbian.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how identity informs perspective and material, but write with complexity so a piece resists being flattened into a single category. Use identity as an informing constellation—one of many factors shaping voice and subject.
